questions.q: Why do superconducting qubits need to be cooled to millikelvin temperatures, rather than just somewhat cold?
options: Both to keep the circuit material superconducting and to suppress ambient thermal microwave photons that could otherwise randomly disturb the qubit's state
Millikelvin temperatures are required only to make the chip physically smaller
Cold temperatures are needed only to slow down the speed of light inside the chip's wiring
It is purely a historical convention with no physical necessity
questions.explain: Two distinct physical reasons both require millikelvin cooling: the wiring must remain superconducting, and thermal photon noise near the qubit's operating frequency must be suppressed enough that it doesn't randomly excite or disturb the qubit.

questions.q: Why does a dilution refrigerator cool in multiple distinct temperature stages rather than in a single step?
options: No single cooling mechanism is efficient across the entire range from room temperature down to millikelvin, so each stage removes the heat load appropriate to its own temperature range
Multiple stages exist purely for aesthetic reasons in the refrigerator's design
Single-stage cooling is prohibited by law for quantum computing hardware
Each stage cools the chip to a slightly warmer temperature than the previous one
questions.explain: Trying to remove all the heat from room temperature to millikelvin with one mechanism would be far too inefficient -- staged cooling lets each stage handle only the smaller remaining heat load passed down from the stage above it.

questions.q: What physical process in the mixing chamber provides the dilution refrigerator's final cooling power?
options: Continuous separation and pumping of a helium-3/helium-4 mixture between a helium-3-rich phase and a helium-3-dilute phase, which absorbs heat similarly to evaporation but remains effective down to millikelvin temperatures
Direct mechanical compression of liquid nitrogen
Rapid spinning of the qubit chip to shed heat via centrifugal force
Combustion of hydrogen gas to generate a cooling vacuum
questions.explain: The 'dilution' in dilution refrigerator refers to this continuous helium-3/helium-4 phase-separation process, which keeps providing cooling power far below where ordinary evaporative cooling would stop working.

questions.q: Why does adding more qubits to a superconducting processor create a genuine wiring-related scaling bottleneck inside the cryostat?
options: Each qubit typically needs its own physical control/readout lines running through every cold stage, and more lines mean more heat load and more consumed physical space, both of which are limited inside the refrigerator
More qubits require the chip to be physically heated instead of cooled
Wiring has no effect on the refrigerator's performance regardless of qubit count
Adding qubits requires removing the mixing chamber entirely
questions.explain: Every additional qubit's control and readout wiring is a real physical object taking up limited cryostat space and carrying real heat load into the cold stages -- this is a genuine physical constraint, not just a cost or complexity inconvenience.

questions.q: What does the lesson identify as one of the central reasons simply 'adding more qubits' to a superconducting chip is a genuine engineering challenge?
options: The dilution refrigerator has finite physical space and finite cooling power at its coldest stage, both of which are consumed by the wiring each additional qubit requires
Superconducting qubits become chemically unstable once more than a few dozen are placed on one chip
There is no real challenge -- more qubits can always be added by simply making the chip larger with no other constraints
Adding qubits requires abandoning superconducting materials entirely
questions.explain: The refrigerator's finite cold-stage space and cooling power, combined with the per-qubit wiring heat load, form a real physical scalability bottleneck that fabricating a bigger chip alone does not solve.
